blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A platform team runs one fixed checklist (lint, test, report) over forty unrelated systems. A colleague wants an adaptive planner for each because it is more capable. What is the best answer?

options.says: Ruled out because capability has a price: "Agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance."

options.text: Use one planner for the forty of them in a single shared session instead
options.says: Ruled out because the systems do not interact, so nothing is gained by a shared planner: "A fixed chain, run once for each item".

options.text: Use the plain sequence on each
options.says: Known steps and independent items call for the simplest shape.

options.text: Use a pass for each plus a cross pass
options.says: Ruled out because a cross pass is for items that affect each other: "Items that do not (forty services, each given the same checklist) need only the chain, run forty times."

questions.stem: A team's adaptive investigation asks the planner for each next step, but shows it only its own earlier plan text and not what the earlier work produced. After a few steps the plan drifts away from the true state of the code. What fixes it?

options.text: Ask it to restate the goal more carefully before each step
options.says: Ruled out because the source of the drift is what it is shown: "a plan that is made from the model's own previous guesses drifts".

options.text: Plan every step up front and run the plan unchanged
options.says: Ruled out because an up-front plan has no results to use: "the plan is made before any ground truth exists".

options.text: Give it the result of each action, such as a test run
options.says: The planner needs ground truth from each step, not its own earlier guesses.

options.text: Switch to a fixed chain that runs the same steps every time
options.says: Ruled out because a chain has no planner to drift and no way to use what a step found: "If step two finds that step three is pointless, the chain runs step three."

questions.stem: A source file has four thousand lines, which is too long for one pass. By the practice's own rule for long files, how should it be handled?

options.text: Send its first part only and skip the remainder
options.says: Ruled out because the rest of the file would never be reviewed: "A file that does not fit a pass of its own is cut into parts of a fixed number of lines".

options.text: Summarise the file in one sentence and use the sentence in its place
options.says: Ruled out because a sentence does not carry the interfaces: "what the file offers (the functions and types others use, with their parameters)".

options.text: Send the whole file anyway and trust the pass to keep its parts connected
options.says: Ruled out because the whole file brings back the problem of the split: "spends that budget on text before the review begins".

options.text: Cut it into labelled parts and join their summaries into one entry
options.says: Parts keep each pass small and the summary joins them.

origin.section: A file that is too long
